analysis: Changes are diagnostic-only. DaemonStateFile.swift (head lines 88-91, 325-337, 368, 404) adds an optional CoordinatorConnection struct (connected, since, connections) to the daemon state snapshot. It is purely local and optional, so older files still decode. The fields are non-secret booleans, a timestamp and a counter. The JSON file is written with data.write(.atomic) (line 638) and no explicit permissions. That is pre-existing behavior, and the new fields add no sensitive data. DoctorRunner.swift adds trafficDiagnostic(_:) and a call at about patch line 112-116. It renders ServingReadiness.Verdict into a read-only Diagnostic. The call is gated on stateFresh, which requires doctorDaemonProcessMatches, so a stale file or a mismatched process is not trusted. The verdict is displayed only and never gates serving, grants authorization, or touches coordinator authorization (A-016, T-052/T-053). The diagnostic message reuses advice text and detail strings; I could not see ServingReadiness.verdict, whose implementation is not in the supplied evidence. Open question: does ServingReadiness derive 'authorized' only from coordinator-supplied authorization state, with the expiry check applied by currentProviderAuthorization, rather than from the unauthenticated local state file? The state file is user-writable at same-UID trust level, so a same-user local actor could spoof the display. That is a UI-trust limitation within the existing TB-003 assumptions, not a serving-permission regression, because the daemon and coordinator remain authoritative. Also check that DoctorRunner does not mislabel 'eligible' where T-052 warns that shadow or legacy labels are not serving permission. No regression identified in the supplied source. Residual uncertainty is limited to the unseen ServingReadiness implementation.
